utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Good morning, Madam Registrar. Could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. For the record, General Pandurevic is absent today. He notified us previously about this and he has also communicated to us his waiver so that the proceedings can go ahead with -- in his absence. Defence teams, it's Mr. Haynes who is absent and Ms. Nikolic and Mr. Meek. Prosecution, I notice Mr. McCloskey. And I take it there are no preliminaries and all technical problems have been dealt with satisfactorily for which I thank you the technicians, and I think we may proceed. Good morning to you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome back. I hope you had time to relax. Mr. McCloskey will finish his examination-in-chief shortly and then we proceed to the cross-examinations. Mr. McCloskey, good morning to you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, General. I want to go over the diagram that you and I worked with a bit in my office. I apologise, it's more of a working document than a really good exhibit but I think it will serve our purposes. It's in e-court now at P02828 but if I can give the general the original so he can take a look at it, it might come up better on the ELMO too. I don't -- let's see how that e-court one looks like. Now, this is, when it comes up, a diagram of one of the long office buildings in Crna Rijeka that we are aware of and what I've done here is, as you recall, General, is I blanked out several of the offices of the higher ranking people and you filled in the blank spots and then we circled the spots that you filled in. So if we can go over just briefly the spots that you filled in in circles and just tell us what it is, let's start off with you've put glavni ulaz. What is that, that first circle on the top?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to numbers 5 and 6 or some other circle which I don't see? I don't know which you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where it says glavni ulaz?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry. For us, can you tell us what that means, what that indicated when you wrote that in?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is two wooden sheds at the beginning next to each other. Left to the one that is drawn here, there was another one the same size and shape. Every shed had two entrances, one that I denoted as the main entrance was the main in that -- in the respect that the first office from the entrance was the office that I shared with General Mladic. In the corridor in front of the office there was a courier who received people, announced visitors, and that's why I marked this as the main entrance. At the very bottom, there is another entrance which was mostly used by the auxiliary personnel, drivers and others, and it was next to the toilets and bathrooms. There were two entrances, but I marked this as the main entrance because this was also the main reception. Do you want me to go on commenting on other rooms as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Why don't you comment on what you've written in in that big oval for room number 5. What did you write there and what is that room that's divided by dots?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This room marked by 5, this was the office that I shared with General Mladic. We wanted to be efficient in utilising the space and that's why we shared that one office, because if he was there, I wasn't, and vice versa, or if we were there together in the Main Staff, then we shared that one office because we had to cooperate and that saved us a lot of time, saved us running across the corridor, and I put "Miletic" in the brackets. When Miletic arrived in the operations administration, he worked with us but when I wasn't there, he would sit in my chair, so to speak. He worked from my office. The next room is number 6, and it says the blue hall. At the beginning of the war this was the room used by General Gvero. In 1995, we equipped that hall with some furniture and we turned it into a little conference room for the inner staffs meeting or for the reception of visitors who came to visit. That's when we moved General Gvero to number 7. General Tolimir was in number 8, as far as I can remember. And the room under number 5 with a dotted line, that was my rest room. There was a door between number 5 and the dotted line. In the evening or during the night when I finished my work or if I wanted to have a rest during the day, I would use this room to rest. On the other screen, I can see a bit further. Room number 4, I don't remember what it was. I suppose that this was for the signals chief, Colonel Radomir Prole, and then number 8, General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we get the diagram up a bit so we can get the other half of the -- where he's talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, keep going, excuse me, General.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 3, this was the biggest room in this prefabricated building and it was used to accommodate the operations centre of the Main Staff. We are talking about the above-the-ground command post, the command post which was not under the ground. The person in charge in that room was General Miletic, and that's where he spent most of his time working there. In addition to him the centre also has the duty team of the Main Staff. The head of the duty team was always an operative, either General Miletic or one of his assistants, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, General, I'm sorry, I may have missed it, but was that number 2 that you talked about, the duty room?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I'm talking about number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry, that's my fault. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the operations centre of the Main Staff. In addition to the operative representatives of all the assistant commanders were present in that room at all times, as well as the chiefs of administration, different administrations, there were always anywhere between 10 and 12 people there at any time. This was the duty team, and if General Mladic or myself or Miletic were absent or any of General Mladic's assistants were absent or if we were all absent, then this team was capable of dealing with the current situations on the front line. This is all I can say about room number 3. Room number 9, which is parallel to number 3, as far as I can remember, this was reserved for the chiefs of the various branches. I know that Colonel Nedjelko Trkulja was there. Somebody else was with him, but I can't remember who, especially in view of the fact that I didn't spend much time in the Main Staff in 1995 and I didn't have much contact with these people. Room number 10 was reserved for the chief of engineers, Colonel Mihajlo Djurdjevic I believe his name was, and Colonel Dragisa Mashal [phoen], who had his bed there but otherwise he was with me all the time on the western front. Room number 2, I can't remember who occupied that room. Room number 11, there was Colonel Pancic there. He was the chief of the artillery rocket units and the anti-aircraft defence. He replaced General Miletic. He took over his position. Room number 1, originally it said Milovanovic here but somebody reversed the entrances. This room was for the helicopter pilots, the command helicopter pilots. We had three or four helicopters and the pilots mostly slept in this room. Room number 12 was for the chief of the air force and the anti-aircraft defence administration. He was one of General Mladic's assistants. The next room below number 1 was the bathroom and across the corridor the last room on the right-hand side was the toilet, and you can see the letters WC on that room. The next-door prefabricated house accommodated the services, various offices, even the outpatient's clinic and I believe that the security administration was accommodated there and I can't remember who else. This was the next door prefabricated house and I don't think it's that important for this case. Save for the security administration, I believe everybody else was auxiliary personnel. In the course of the war sometime in 1993, a third prefabricated house was erected. It was very similar in size and shape to the previous two, and since the Main Staff was enlarged and reinforced, the third house accommodated auxiliary personnel. Since that house was new, people competed as to who would be accommodated there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. On this second auxiliary house that you said housed the security, was that where Colonel Beara and Colonel Salapura were?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Beara, yes, I believe he was there. I'm sure he was. And as for Colonel Salapura, he switched between the houses. I don't know why. I believe that the chief of sector, General Tolimir, at the beginning of the war, wanted to have Salapura next to him. He was in one of the rooms in this prefabricated house that we see on the screen now and then he moved to the next house and I don't know what happened when the third house was erected. At the beginning of the war Salapura was in this house that is in front of us and later on he went to the other house as well. Salapura was rarely in the Main Staff. He was the chief of the intelligence administration. He mostly worked in -- with the units, with corps commands. He was mainly on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And do you remember, and I know you weren't there often, but in July 1995, if General Gvero was working out of that main office or was he working out of some place else, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Save for the 20th June, when we saw Zivanovic off, I was not in staff, and yesterday I told you how I met Gvero, whether I met Gvero, how we contacted, I really I really don't know. I was not there in June [as translated] save for that one day that I told you about yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I think that should be you were not there in July except for that one day. It got translated as June. Would I be correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right. I'm talking about July. I'm talking about the month of July. Only on the 19th, in the evening, and on the 20th, I was in the Main Staff, July, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And one other exhibit I had forgotten to go to yesterday and I don't want to get into it really in detail. It's number 692. It's this line and block chart of the Main Staff. I had given you a big copy of that the other evening to check for us, and you had mentioned we didn't put in a couple of things. Can you just tell us now what that chart needs to have added to it so it is complete? And this isn't going to be very readable but we don't really need it for our purposes. This -- but does this look like -- I can tell you this is a copy of what I gave you, though you can't really tell from this picture.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a copy of this document, but maybe it would be better to put the A4 format on the screen. This is A3 and it cannot fit onto the screen. Now it's good. Now it's good. I had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will need to zoom in on and off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no need to zoom in but you can scroll up because I lack the bottom part of this sketch. That's good now. Here we miss some Main Staff units that are linked with the commander. There is the 65th Regiment and there is the 10th Sabotage Detachment. That's okay. But there is no signals regiment which was also a Main Staff unit. And there is no guards brigade as a Main Staff unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: To complete this diagram, we need to add those two units; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There should be together with the 65th Protection Regiment, then the 10th Sabotage Detachment. I had it on my sketch. I added by hand some squares and I added these two units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We'll update that diagram and, Your Honours, we will get you I think hard copies of this so that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We've seen it -- I think we've seen it before already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And I think it's part of the indictment, but it wasn't my intention to go over it now but I did want to clear that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, another -- just one last question. Do you remember we had talked about the extension number for your office in Banja Luka, and I had -- do you remember the extension number you had at the time in 1995 in your office?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we talked in Banja Luka, I couldn't remember. You jogged my memory. This was number 155, which was in the directory, and it was attached to my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as you correctly state, I asked you if you -- if 155 sounded familiar, so I did jog your memory in that way; is that -- that's -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As you sit here today, that is your memory, not me -- not my testimony; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I subsequently checked, I consulted with some people after you'd left, and I realised that that was my number, 155.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much, General Milovanovic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. McCloskey. Have you agreed amongst yourself who is going first? Mr. Zivanovic, could you kindly introduce yourself to General Milovanovic? How much time do you reckon --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: 20 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 20 minutes. That's what you intimated, but I just wanted a confirmation of that. Thank you. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, General. I represent Mr. Vujadin Popovic in these proceedings. My name is Zoran Zivanovic. I would kindly ask you to look at an exhibit that was shown to you by the Prosecutor. The number is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a regular combat report which was sent by the command of the 5th Engineers Battalion to the command of the Drina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2672, 2672.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to item 1 that the Prosecutor read to you yesterday. It reads, "The -- a large group of enemy was infiltrated in the sectors of Pobrdje Brdo and Konjevic Polje. The units of the a 5th Engineers Battalion and the MUP resisted the enemy successfully." Please pay attention to this second sentence. "A total of 1.000 to 1.500 enemy civilians and soldiers were either arrested or killed." Yesterday the Prosecutor read to you this: "About 1.000 to 1.500 enemy civilians and soldiers were arrested and killed."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, there is an official CLSS translation of this in English, and because the nature of the document, I think we need to use this and not put the translation on the booth interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's hear what the witness has to say. Don't answer the question right now. I take it that you wish to address the Chamber. Go ahead, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, could we remove this drawing from the left side of the screen, because it's distracting me and I cannot follow the interpretation or speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Our usher is going to assist you. Mr. McCloskey, both the English version and the B/C/S version are official documents, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, the -- I have no problem with the B/C/S version or the English version, but what's happening is when he reads the B/C/S version, the translators are giving it a different English interpretation than the CLSS because it's not an easy document to translate, and that's putting a very difficult burden on them. This document has spent a lot of time with CLSS to get it right and he will be answering a different question than I asked him on the same document unless we stay with this English version. That's -- so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait, wait, wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have no problem with him asking in his language, reading it in his language but when it gets translated, when they are quoting the document we need to have this document in front of the translators so when they translate it, they are consistent with CLSS. Otherwise, our record is going to be a complete mess.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we have a debate over the translation, that's fine, but we shouldn't do it in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before we hand down our decision, I noticed earlier on, Madam Fauveau, for example, amongst others, do you wish to address the Chamber? Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm not saying that the interpretation we received is exact, but I agree with the Prosecutor that the text in the original is difficult because the text in original is completely unclear, but the Prosecution calls the CLSS translation faithful and correct, but in my view, it is not completely inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyone else wishes to address the Chamber? Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Quite frankly there are two points that we should look at. Draft in English as my colleagues indicated shows that it's a draft translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I had noted Madam Fauveau should have said that it is completely inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not completely. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we're going to have --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And secondly --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- without interruption --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- a debate about this --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Without interruption. Secondly --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- it should not be in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But the OTP started the debate in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but what the OTP was a very simple proposition or submission. What we are stating now is something different. General, do you understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can I ask you to remove your headphones, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I say something? Because I see that we are wasting time on an issue. I think the interpreters are under attack here, but yesterday when this document was first presented to me, I followed the interpretation very attentively because I had a misunderstanding with the Prosecutor regarding one sentence in this directive, number 4, regarding connecting words, commas, et cetera. In my headset I received the interpretation exactly as it is in the document. "Around 1.000 to 1.500 enemy civilians and soldiers were arrested killed," without any full stop, any comma between the words "arrested" and "killed." I only have great doubts about the literacy of the person who wrote this because it would be logical for a comma or the word "and" the connecting word "and" to be between "arrested" and "killed." The interpreters gave me a verbatim translation, and please do not blame them. I paid great attention to this and the interpreters said, "Around 1.000 to 1500 enemy civilians and soldiers were arrested killed."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, one moment, please, because Mr. Ostojic hasn't finished as yet. Can I ask to you remove your headphones, please. Do you intend to address the Chamber as well, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Then I think the witness needs to leave the courtroom because he will be addressing the courtroom in B/C/S and he will be understanding what you're saying -- or what you will be saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ostojic, Mr. Zivanovic, but if any one of you is contending that the translation that Mr. McCloskey referred to is not accurate, please indicate exactly where, according to you, it is not accurate. Mr. Ostojic goes first.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. First as I initially stated, the document itself in English clearly identifies it as being a draft translation so it was never put in final form. The Prosecutor does, as we've seen and I think we can see from time to time, there are problems with interpretation that may be critical. This word or this sentence can be turned to mean several things, some were arrested, some may have been killed; or the way the Prosecutor likes the sentence to be read, that they were first arrested and then all of them were killed, which is not what the document says in English or in B/C/S. The problem is that the Prosecutor wants to give a little more credit to the CLCS and say that they have this official kind of cloth about them that whatever they say is accurate. They don't consult with us, they don't consult with the Defence at all on these translations. With all due respect, Your Honours I think it's necessary for such important documents when the Prosecutor takes them where we think a little further than necessary, as in this case, there should have been some consultation with the Defence. There has not been. Secondly, the CLCS department is no better, quite candidly, than the translators that we have here, so for the prosecutors to suggest that we can't translate one sentence after they've translated in excess of 15.000 pages of transcript since the commencement of this trial, I think is something that we should not accept. The translators here on good faith, the oath that they took, took the sentence that Mr. Zivanovic asked and translated it accurately and according to what they heard and what's written before them on the ELMO. There is a disparity as to how someone may or may not interpret this sentence. However, translation's a different thing. When you translate it, you look at the words and do you not come up with the most favourable interpretation that the Prosecution wants, which is what they're doing in this case, so I do object to the Prosecution how they manipulate, in my view, this sentence and how they try to give it a little added credibility to suggest that this is an official translation by some third independent party, when he knows in fact that they themselves have worked with CLCS on other documents and have asked them to revise like the issues with security, it's not called specifically security, it might be called something else, and they've revised that on numerous documents to fit their theory. So we do object to this vigorously, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Zivanovic? Yes, one moment. Mr. McCloskey, do you wish to address -- to respond to Mr. Ostojic now or after hearing Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's probably easier now so I won't get it too confused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. I wish to you address something which is fundamental here. There is a tremendous difference between what appears in the transcript as being the translation or interpretation of Mr. Zivanovic's reading out from the document to the witness, namely, a total of 1.000 to 1.500 enemy civilians and soldiers were either arrested or killed, what -- from what the draft translation that you are relying upon states, and essentially now at the end of it, from what the witness himself stated. So -- because the witness himself is not saying either arrested or killed. He is complaining only that the confusion may arise since there is a comma absent between "arrested" and "killed."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That shows the problem, because I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is what I want to hear submissions about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When he asked the question the interpreters did their best. When the General just read the same B/C/S language, he said "arrested killed" and the only worry as you said was the "and" was mixed -- was out of it, which was much more closely to the English translation. Now, whether the booth was affected by the CLSS translation or whether it was because of the way they heard it as the general spoke, I don't know. The booth knows that when there is a translation up there on the screen or when many times the parties give them the official translation, they read from that so that we don't get into this apples and oranges situation. This document, because of its nature, we wanted to get right and so we spent a fair amount of time -- I can't remember how far it's gone but it -- this is a translation that was done by the CLSS and I'll look into how far, but it's my knowledge of the accurate -- the best they could do. Now, this is a document that's been out forever and of course there is going to be conflict sometimes in translation, and I welcome to work that conflict out but, please, this document's been here forever and it's -- no one had any objection to it. They didn't even object to it when I used it in direct. It's not until now that it's being used and we're getting these translations. We need to resolve these issues earlier. They know the language and they've been very good helping us sort out translation errors, but we need -- have to have this material sorted out beforehand and we need some consistency here. But my point is, this general from the first day I showed him that document said this was a war crime, with whatever this thing said, he said it was a war crime. He looked at the original document. He said it was a war crime in Banja Luka. He said it was a war crime here. So I think that resolves any translation issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please, please, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Look. I've been accused of phoneying up translations to meet my case. I think I can respond to that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Zivanovic first and you after, Madam Fauveau. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wanted and I still want to clarify with the witness one very simple thing, those two sentences, just as I began. I want to tell you on page 71 from 12 to 17 lines of yesterday's transcript, there is a very clear quotation of the statement of Mr. McCloskey where it says that this sentence reads, "1.000 to 1500 enemy civilians and soldiers were arrested and killed." I am not saying that Mr. McCloskey did something like this deliberately. I can even assume that there could have been the word "and," arrested and killed, but I want to see with the witness whether, in addition to the word "and," another word could be possible there. Just one moment. I wish to add, that could be the word "or" which would change the meaning of this sentence completely. And in that case, it would read, "1.000 to 1500 enemy civilians and soldiers were arrested or killed," which to me sounds much more logical than the meaning given it by Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have coloured it completely different from how it -- the question was put, because when you look at the transcript on page 10, line -- lines 14 and 15, what we have on the transcript, and I stand to be corrected if the transcript is not correct, of course, we have not a question, you're not putting to the witness, "Witness, General, how do you read this sentence in the document? Do you read it 'arrested and killed' or 'arrested or killed'? What we have here is an affirmation on your part, please pay attention to the second sentence, "A total of 1.000 to 1.500 enemy civilians and soldiers were either arrested or killed." So what you're putting to the witness is not the possibility of having it either one way or another. You're putting to the witness a statement emerging from the document itself establishing that the 1.000 to 1.500 were either arrested or killed. This is how the transcript presents itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if the --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I didn't give you permission --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- to interject as yet. Please sit down. You'll have your turn, Mr. Ostojic. I mean, I -- there's no way I cannot see you. Yes -- one moment. Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that's precisely the problem with this sentence. My colleague, Mr. Zivanovic, said that he in fact read the sentence as it was in Serbo-Croat. It's not comprehensible and it's a fact that different interpreters interpreted it differently. And that's why in the written translation that we have, we have the word "and" and in this version and in the interpretation we received the word "or" in Serbo-Croat. There is definitely a word missing. But neither the word "and" nor the word "or" exists in the Serbo-Croat original. And I want to say that it's very unfortunate that this document has been here I don't know how long and some people have been convicted on the basis of it due to an erroneous translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that's the -- your contention. You're affirming that it is an erroneous translation. Your version of it could be erroneous too. I mean this is what I understand from the submissions, that while Mr. McCloskey maintains that the draft translation that has been offered is the correct translation, you're maintaining the opposite. What I'm suggesting for the time being, before I hear Mr. Ostojic and I hear you, Mr. McCloskey, is perhaps that rather than relying on translations, you -- we bring the witness in again and you direct him, we'll have the document on the -- he will have the document on the monitor, he will have the paragraph that you specifically want to refer him to, and you ask him what he makes out of that paragraph, what he understands from that paragraph. And that way we'll be avoiding all translation issues unless of course new translation issues arise while what he's saying is being translated to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The position I think is clear enough. I don't think, unless there is something new that you wish to bring to our attention that we need to hear any further on this. I think there is a translation issue here relating to -- regarding this specific part of that paragraph that needs to be resolved. Obviously, we cannot resolve it now and it will need to be resolved through expert, independent translation or -- translation. For the time being what we intend doing is to proceed as we indicated, that, in other words, we will bring the witness in again, you will refer the witness to the paragraph that you had in mind that you had indicated before, without reading any part from it, because the witness can read it himself, it's in his own language, and we will hear what the interpretation will -- you will just ask him what he makes out of that paragraph. Of course, we will be receiving interpretation. We in English, Madam Fauveau in French, and I don't know if there is any other language. And that will of course not prejudice the aspect of then trying to procure or seeking to procure a proper translation of the document, if it is at all possible, because as I understand it, if there is a problem, I think the problem will remain, from what we have heard -- from what we can gather from your submissions, anyway. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just wish to note that I didn't have time to ask this witness a single question. I just quoted those two sentences from the document and I managed to quote the words of Mr. McCloskey that found their way into the transcript, but I had no time to ask the witness a single question. I don't know what actually entered the transcript, the record. I had no time to follow it, but I didn't actually ask the witness any question. I wanted to ask precisely what you are saying, maybe in a slightly different way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No one is blaming you for anything, Mr. Zivanovic. Please don't misread me. What I am saying is the following: When you stood up, started your questions, whichever way you made your statement, because your statement was in B/C/S, it was translated to us in a way which does not conform, which does not tally, with what is contained in the translation that Mr. McCloskey or the Prosecution was relying on -- please, Mr. Ostojic. At that point in time his standing up and objecting was almost the thing to expect. I mean, we are not surprised that he stood up, because the translation of what you read was different from the translation that he has. At that point in time, what emerged clear is that there are two versions that are being provided by way of translation to this part of the document which differ and they differ substantially. So that needs to be kept apart for the time being. We have been made aware of it. Mr. McCloskey relies on the draft translation which I agree with Mr. Ostojic is not an official translation. It's just a draft translation. Those of you who have spoken from the Defence side maintain that it doesn't say so, that the translation is not correct, it says something different, it says either "or," as you maintain, like Mr. McCloskey relies on an "and" rather than an "or." So that needs to be sorted out, but I don't think we can sort it out, because we don't understand the language in the first place, and I don't think any further submissions from your side will help us because the witness himself now will be asked to state what he makes of that statement. If that comes out, we may have again some translation problems and then we will sort it out. Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, thank you, and Your Honours, I would just like to clarify for the record on page 18 when you recited what Mr. Zivanovic said, if we look closely on page 10 when he started the questioning, 16 and 17, both those lines, he specifically started his question by first reading the quote and the translator said either "or." Then he proceeds to say "however, the Prosecutor told you," and he uses the word "and." So just so the record's clear, Mr. Zivanovic I think in my view did ask either "or" and "and" was ready to put the question. It's not as I hear now that Mr. Zivanovic only gave him one option and invited him to answer, but in fact I think the record is plain that he gave him both options. I just want the record or at least my view of the record to be placed on the record in this manner. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we have to stop it at that. I mean, I don't think Mr. Zivanovic needs anyone else to defend him because we haven't accused him of anything in the first place, and I think it's obvious that he may have intended to proceed with a further question. The thing is what is relevant is not that. What is relevant is that at that point in time a divergence between one version and another emerged that needed to be addressed, full stop. Yes, Mr. McCloskey, and that will be the end of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could -- we have interviewed the author of this document and he has -- was asked about it. If I could -- I'd like to put him on the witness list. It's not someone I put on the witness list before, but given this controversy, I will just alert you I'll put him on the 65 ter motion witness list to help us assist in this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please file an appropriate motion, if you deem it necessary. And we will hear what the Defence teams have to say about that. Madam Usher -- one moment, one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Usher, could you be kind enough to bring the witness in, please. And Mr. Zivanovic, if you don't mind, I think I will put the question myself to make it easier for you to proceed afterwards. And as I said, this will leave the whole issue unprejudiced, which version of the two is the correct one, if there is a correct version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, General, for being patient with us. We are ready to proceed. Do you have in front of you on the screen the document that we were -- you were referred to earlier on? That is the one which has at the top right -- no, I was going to refer to the ERN number -- 04392942? Do you have it in front of you? Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do, and yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So could I please ask you to read the first paragraph? You don't need to read it aloud. Just read it. And then tell us what you understand from it. We are particularly interested in the last part of that paragraph, the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last sentence reads, "A total of 1.000 to 1500 enemy civilians and soldiers were arrested killed." I am not sure what you want me to say about this sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How do you understand it? That's all we are interested in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if the report is correct, although I doubt its accuracy, like I said it yesterday to the Prosecutor, this is war crime. I expanded that a little in Banja Luka. I told him that this was a war crime, be it a one prisoner or 1.001 prisoners. I doubt the accuracy of this document for this reason. It says here, about 1.000 to 1500. The author of the report cannot go amiss by 500 people. This means that the report was drafted without any verification on the ground. And as I was reflecting on this document during my preparations for the testimony, I tried to establish a link between this report and the report that the Main Staff sent to the Supreme Command, and I did not find it anywhere that the Main Staff reported to the Supreme Command on this. And now a question imposes itself and I cannot answer it, I cannot establish the facts. The question is whether the corps command conveyed this report to the Main Staff on that same evening, which was the 14th of July. I can't see the heading of this report, so I can't be sure of the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Can you please -- yeah. Now you can see the date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This was on the 14th of July. I was right. In the report by the Main Staff, dated the 14th of July, sent to the Supreme Command, this information is missing. There is no data or information to this effect, as we see here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I hand you back to Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: General, you said that in your opinion, an illiterate person drafted this report or somebody who was not very literate, at least. Did I understand you well, and is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because that person is not very well-versed in the grammar of his language.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, the fact that the person doesn't know his grammar, can this be reflected in the fact that there is no connecting word between the words "arrested" and "killed" and the connecting word should have been either "and" or "or," and in other words, the sentence should read -- and I'm going to quote to you two variations -- the first one would be "a total of 1.000 to 1.500 civilians and soldiers were arrested and killed" or, in the second variation, "arrested or killed."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We are going back into the old problem. I thought we'd solved that with your questions. Because the more he starts quoting the document, the more we're going to get confusion. The way that came out, I don't have an objection to but I thought we'd resolved this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, we made it clear that if there is a way of solving the translation issue, we will try to solve it through independent translation. You're trying to get the witness to solve it for us, and the witness has already made it clear that there being a comma absent there, he's not in a position to state whether it's "and" or "or." So why put the question again and reopen the whole issue? I see that the general wishes it address us again before you are given back the floor, Mr. Zivanovic. Yes, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I understand myself as a witness here. I'm not a grammar analyst or a military analyst, for that matter. I wanted to seek your protection in that respect and I wanted to ask you whether I am obliged to answer such questions. A witness is either a participant or an eyewitness of an event. To ask for me to comment upon the grammar of this document, I don't think, is appropriate. You asked me for my comment and my comment was, if this report is correct, if it's accurate, then this is a war crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to say a few words? The general has provided his interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime I wish to assure the general that there are four of us here, differing in size, but we are all in a position to protect you and we will, General. And Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have put the question to the general because the general provided his opinion of the document and I didn't understand this as a bad interpretation but a poor literacy. He did tell us that the person was not very literate and I just put to him the two words that might have been omitted. This was not the matter of a bad interpretation or translation but the interpretation of the document by the general that either one or possibly two different words might have been omitted for -- from the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the general has given you that answer already throughout his previous statements, so please proceed with your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: General, does it arise from the report that you see in front of you that some fighting went on there?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anybody can conclude that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether this arises from the word in the first sentence, and the words are that the units of the 5th Battalion and the MUP resisted the enemy successfully?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. Can you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to quote the whole sentence.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see the sentence. I can see the sentence. You don't have to quote it, but I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The Prosecution agrees that there was some fighting going on at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So that's a stipulation. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see from this report that the enemy suffered any losses during all this time? Does this arise from a report worded in this particular way?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that during the fighting anybody suffered any losses. I see from the second part that people were arrested killed, and we go back to your original question whether people were arrested and killed or arrested or killed. However, one may understand it that a thousand to 1.500 people were arrested and killed after the fighting, because while the fighting is going on, you do not arrest people. You capture them as prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: From the interpretation of this report, it arises that the enemy did not suffer any losses during the fighting because everybody was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I don't know that. I don't know whether they were all arrested. I don't know that between 1.000 and 1.500 were arrested and I don't know how many of them were there in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And can you see how many were killed during the fighting, whether anybody was killed during the fighting?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I've told you that I can't see from this sentence that anybody was killed during the fighting. Somewhere towards the end where it says losses, but I can't see it on the screen right now, I'm afraid, it seems that it read -- can you scroll up a little, if you will?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I was not referring to the losses of the VRS but the enemy losses in the fighting. I was referring to the enemy losses, and the enemy is the person opposed to the person who drafted the report.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I believe that it says here as follows: "The Battalion did not suffer any losses," and I can't see it on the screen, but as far as I can remember, the battalion did not suffer any losses. It is certain that the Serb side did not suffer any losses, that there were no -- there was nobody killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask you that.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me whether the enemy suffered any losses. I can't see it here. It is not written in here. I can't claim with certainty that they were or that they weren't. If I had been there, if I had been an eyewitness, I would have known. If I'd participated in this fighting, I would have known, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In this particular case, in this specific case it arises from the report that the enemy side had at least 1500 men and probably even more. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you think that there were fewer than that or less people than that, according to this report?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it could not have been less than that because 1500 were arrested. There could have been more.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When it says here that they successfully resisted the enemy group, I suppose that this was an armed resistance. Does it seem logical to you, as an experienced officer, that the enemy does not suffer any losses if there is armed resistance?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, am I supposed to answer this question? Do I have to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're asking him for an opinion, Mr. Zivanovic, which it's not the case. So please proceed to your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: General, I'll ask you to tell me something about the order that was shown to you yesterday by the Prosecutor. And the number is 2748 -- I apologise. It is number 29 on the Prosecutor's list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Directive, not an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's that, yes. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, yesterday we heard that in 1995 -- I'm not asking about this particular thing, I'm asking you about 1995 -- we heard that both in Srebrenica and in Zepa, there were armed formations of the BiH army that were active and that they were deployed among the civilian population; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to what you know, during their activities, did they use the civilian population as a human shield, to protect themselves, to defend themselves from attacks?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was typical behaviour of the Muslim army in the enclaves. I wouldn't want to go back to the origin and the essence of the enclaves, Srebrenica, Zepa, Gorazde, Tuzla, Sarajevo and Bihac. The fact remains that the Muslim armed forces in the enclaves were not disarmed and the UNPROFOR was supposed to do that, and one does not have to present any evidence. It suffices to look at the signatures of the commander of the 28th Division of the so-called army of Bosnia-Herzegovina with the commander's signature, Naser Oric and his Chief of Staff whose name I don't know, I've forgotten it. In Srebrenica, in 1993 in the month of May, I believe on the 8th of May when the enclave was proclaimed and when General Mladic and General Halilovic as the commanders of the warring parties signed the agreement on the demilitarisation of Srebrenica, UNPROFOR accepted the task to be the guarantor of the realisation of this agreement and they were supposed to disarm the remaining Muslim soldiers who had withdrawn into Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: General, I apologise for interrupting. My time for the cross-examination is rather limited. That's why I would like to ask you to tell me this: Were the civilian population used as the human shield? Did the BiH army use the civilian population, in the enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica, use the civilian population as a human shield?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One of the covenants of the agreement on the demilitarisation was violated and that covenant was that civilian and military targets should not have been mixed, but the military was mixed with the civilians and we could not target the army because we would have targeted the civilians as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This behaviour by the BiH army, was it the same before the enclaves were proclaimed? And I'm talking about 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer this question because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Who is going next? Mr. Krgovic. Could you introduce yourself with the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Milovanovic. I represent General Gvero in this trial. Since we have seven to eight minutes to the break, maybe if you prefer, we can take the break now or maybe we can start and use up these remaining seven, eight minutes, if that would perhaps allow to you focus after all the grammatical interpretations.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not up to me. It's up to the Presiding Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. I was going to pass the same comment. It would have been more appropriate if you had addressed that invitation to the Chamber, which we would have gladly accepted, as we are doing now. We'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic? Yes, one moment, Mr. Krgovic, because I see --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I do have a preliminary matter outside the presence of the witness that I wanted to address the Chamber, if I may. There is three points specifically. First, on page 17, line 8 and 9, when the Prosecutor said there's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. 17?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Page 17, line 8 and 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When the Prosecution suggests that he's being accused of phoneying up the documents, that's not accurate. I spoke to Mr. McCloskey. That's not our position. No one is suggesting that, but I think when he stood up and said it was the official translation, we counter on that. Just so the record's clear on that, there is no accusation against the Prosecutor on phoneying up the documents here. Second point I'd like to make is that we think, or at least I do, respectfully, that the Prosecution suggests at times in his argument that the -- or is trying to shape the Defence. The Defence at least for Mr. Beara and for myself, has never been from the outset, nor is it today that if you arrest and kill civilians and soldiers that it's not a war crime. That's not what we're asking this Trial Chamber to decide, as the Court knows. It's not proper for the Prosecution to continuously say that it is a war crime and on the other hand perhaps this Court should ask the witness is arresting a civilian or a soldier, is that a war crime? Is in combat killing a soldier, is that a war crime? So and I just want to draw the Court's attention to it, because he said it and I didn't have an opportunity to respond to him and I think we're clear on this point. The third point, the third point, if I may, if I may, with respect to the author of this document, 65 ter number 2672, who's the deputy commander major, we believe and we can stipulate that the Prosecution with the Court's permission does not need to go and file a motion and that they should add him to the list and we'd like to hear from this witness, if that's okay with the Court, unless the Court feels this also needs to be done in writing. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we need to hear you, Mr. McCloskey, on this. First point made by Mr. Ostojic, we don't need to comment upon. The second thing, I don't think it's either for the Prosecution or for the witness to establish what is a war crime or not. It's us ultimately that need to decide that. You're free to ask the witness any question you like during your cross-examination, but I think we wouldn't entertain having the opinion of the witness as to what constitutes a war crime or not. The third statement that you -- or third point that you made, do we take it as being only the position of accused Beara? Because there are other seven -- six accused together with him, who have not opened their mouth on the matter as yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So that's our position. Does anyone of the other defence teams wish to make a statement on this last point made by Mr. Ostojic in relation to this would-be witness, 65 ter witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have spoken to my learned colleagues and we are all in agreement with the last point that it isn't necessary to file the motion. We don't have an objection to it but if the Court permits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is no objection, obviously there is no need to file a motion. Permission is granted. In any case, we wanted to make it clear that even if no motion was forthcoming, we tended towards requesting the presence of this witness ourselves. So let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Speaking for myself, if the OTP is not calling that witness, we are minded to call him as a Chamber witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's the position of all of us. Mr. Krgovic will now proceed with the cross-examination, but first we need the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we are going to proceed with the cross-examination of Mr. Krgovic, who is appearing for General Gvero. Go ahead, Mr. Krgovic. You requested two hours and a half. Do you still need that much time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think I will use just half the time that I envisaged originally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, you may proceed. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning again, General. I will try during my cross-examination to phrase my questions in such a way as to allow you to answer with a yes or no. If a clarification is necessary, please do explain, but to speed up the proceedings, I will try to phrase my questions in that way. General, during the examination-in-chief, you mentioned seven assistant commanders in the Main Staff of the VRS. Out of those seven, one was General Gvero. Do you remember saying that in responding to the Prosecutor's questions?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The exact title of General Gvero was assistant for morale, information, religious and legal affairs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The exact title was chief of sector for morale, religious and legal affairs and at the same time assistant commander for the same affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In that capacity, the chief of those administrations and assistant commander, General Gvero was not a position to issue orders, just like all the others, all the other assistant commanders?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single assistant, whenever General Mladic was there, could issue orders. If General Mladic wasn't there, then I was there so none of the other assistants could issue executive orders. They could issue executive orders only within the purview of their respective sectors, such as order a unit to process such and such information, but no combat orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: At any case, in view of your explanation, those assistant commanders or chiefs of sectors were not called commanders, they were referred to either as assistant commanders or chiefs of sectors? In all communications they were referred to in that way?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. Which commanders?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I mean assistant commanders or chiefs of sectors, they were not addressed as commanders?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Even I wasn't addressed as commander or referred to as commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this, General, because here, there have been some suggestions and opinions voiced by some experts according to which assistant commanders were treated as commanders. That's the reason I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an erroneous interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Can you explain why, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any Prosecution expert or witness who's ever suggested an assistant commander is a -- somehow a commander. So if he has something specific, which I'm sure he does, I would appreciate it because that's never been our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. McCloskey. What are you specifically referring to, Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. General Smith claims precisely that, in the proposal submitted to us by the Prosecution. I can find the relevant page, just to inform the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I've no objection if he can be specific so the general's answering specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but we still have pending the open question as to whether General Smith will be admitted as an expert witness apart from a witness to the facts, but if you have no objection to Mr. Krgovic referring specifically to his expert report which has not yet been admitted, then perhaps he can proceed. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, please go ahead. Make specific reference to the part of the report so that we know exactly which part it and we can follow, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot find it right now. I'll come back to this question later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more thing, General, regarding the chief of sector or assistant commander position. I would like to put it to you that in this title, assistant for some particular kind of affair, in that title there is an exact description of the job performed by that assistant. That's my reading. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The name of the position describes the jurisdiction of that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And it's not possible that an assistant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My sympathy for the interpreters. They are finding it very difficult to catch up with you because you're not even allowing each other to finish question or answer. Please allow a short pause between question and answer, and that applies to both of you, so that the interpreters can do their job properly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, and it's not possible for one assistant to take over the functions of another assistant, in keeping with the rules of service and the doctrine of the army of Republika Srpska? For instance, for General Gvero to take over the functions of General Tolimir, that was not possible, and that did not happen, did it?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not possible for the simple reason that, for instance, General Gvero does not know the job of General Tolimir. I was not able to do that job either, although I was supposed to be knowledgeable about all these things. I couldn't take over the functions of General Gvero. I could have made speeches to the troops to raise their morale but not in the same style as General Gvero did, and it never happened during the war that one chief of sector took over the job of another, because every chief of sector has his own assistant, and in the absence of the chief of sector, the assistant takes over, just as I took over when General Mladic left the zone of the theatre of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Another thing I want to ask you: As you understood it at the time, concerning the position of the -- of General Gvero, his job as a chief of morale was to make speeches to the troops, to raise their morale, to monitor the level of morale, unit by unit, and to receive reports about cases of desertion, violations of discipline and such, and to take care that the readiness of troops to perform missions and assignments be satisfactory. Does that appropriately describe his functions, as far as morale is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I mentioned the making of the speeches, I was speaking figuratively, to somehow describe the functions of General Gvero, but that was not his main job. His main job and his main problem was to build up the morale of the troops of Republika Srpska, and that is a much broader job than just making speeches. His other function had to do with religious affairs, and that had nothing to do with Gvero making troops pray but to establish contacts with religious communities, to enable troops to declare themselves as belonging to one faith or another. And another segment of his activities was legal affairs, namely, creating military courts, monitoring their work, but not interference in their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Military courts, from 1994, fell under the Ministry of Defence and only the section -- the only thing that the section for legal affairs did was receive criminal reports indicating the number of infractions and criminal acts and monitoring how they affected morale. Did I understand correctly the purview of this sector for legal affairs?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the very beginning of the war, from the very moment they were established, military courts were supposed to be under the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska, but they were not, in fact, because the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska was not equipped for that, just as it was not equipped to issue military directives, as I said yesterday. I remember very clearly one evening General Gvero received an explicit assignment from General Mladic to establish military courts, and they were established. But it didn't matter. I mean, it doesn't matter that I don't remember their locations now. Gvero did it, sometime in 1994. I don't remember the exact month. Supposedly, the Ministry of Defence finally got equipped to lead military courts and from that moment on, they fell under their purview, but the functions of General Gvero in legal affairs did not stop. What he did concerning military courts was to monitor the work of military courts in contact with an appropriate section in the Ministry of Defence. But legal affairs also cover more than that. They cover all those shortcomings and deficiencies in the work of the army that are not subject to prosecution, such as violations of discipline, disciplinary infractions, and that is one of the indicators of the state of morale in a unit. If, for instance, one brigade has 50 disciplinary infractions in the course of a month while another unit has ten, that means that the morale of the unit with ten infractions is better than the morale of the unit which has 50. So Gvero and his sector focus on the unit which has the most problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Another component of his work was that the general and his sector were in charge of protocol, that is, organising celebrations, St. Vitus day commemorations, ceremonies, receiving foreign representatives, that is when somebody needs to see the commander, he would organise that meeting, et cetera. That was also his job?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Organising these military festivities and ceremonies was something done with a view to boosting morale. Whether General Gvero organised some artistic ensemble to entertain the troops or whether he was organising festivities on another occasion, it doesn't matter. It's all done in all armies in the world. By entertaining the troops, you raise morale. As far as protocol is concerned, in receiving various delegations, that was not the exclusive purview of General Gvero, because this was handled by people who were receiving a certain delegation in their sector. General Gvero, for instance, had nothing to do with military factories producing a certain kind of equipment. It was handled in that case by the chief of logistics. Or if a representative of the UNPROFOR was coming to the staff or another cooperating armed force, Gvero again had nothing to do with it. It was handled by the staff sector. That is the secretary of the commander of the Main Staff. What I'm trying to say is that it was not Gvero's obligation and responsibility to prepare all kinds of meetings for the Main Staff or personalities of the Main Staff with other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And in particular, it was not his responsibility to liaise with the UNPROFOR on a permanent basis?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you say no, you mean to say that what I said is right, it was not his responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, you are creating problems for me, and I am creating problems for the interpreters. This thing in front of me is continuing to type, and I cannot answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. I think his answer is clear enough, Mr. Krgovic. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The very position of General Gvero at the Main Staff was such that in view of his functions, he had no influence on command, the conduct of operations, or the making of important decisions. He was not the crucial personality who could affect the decision making or command or the execution of operations. Do you agree with this position?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree with that position. General Gvero did not have a decisive influence, but all of us had influence on decision-making. I mentioned yesterday that the Main Staff took its decisions collectively. Therefore, it is certain that in the preceding debate, before the commander says, "I have hereby decided," all of us had the right to present our proposals, our positions, our opinions, and depending on the extent to which the commander accepted our input, all of us had certain influence but none of us seven assistant commanders had a decisive influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe I phrased my question a bit clumsily. I'm speaking about command, about the professional aspect, the conduct of operations, the issuing of orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That's multi-facetted question. I think we're better off if we have individual specific questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Agreed. Mr. Krgovic, please, the suggestion is that you approach these one by one and not cumulatively, as you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milovanovic, did General Gvero have command experience and skills that would allow him to suggest to the commander how to conduct an operation, in which way, and all those professional military aspects? Could he suggest that to the commander?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Same objection, Your Honour. All those professional military aspects? I mean, clearly, there are aspects of his job that he's qualified to talk about that are part of a combat organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. McCloskey. On the other hand, I think for the time being, the witness can concentrate on the first part of the question and then if he can enlighten us on the profession -- all those professional military aspects, if he wishes to address that, he can. Otherwise, Mr. Krgovic would need to be specific. Can you start answering the question, General? The question is: Did General Gvero have command experience and skills that would allow him to suggest to the commander how to conduct an operation and in which way? Let's stick to that first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Every general, by virtue of the fact that he was promoted into general, loses his branch designation. Up to the rank of colonel, we are all colonels of infantry, artillery, armoured and mechanised units, and let me not enumerate further the branches of service. But by virtue of being promoted into general, every general is practically promoted into a general military commander. He can command any type of unit, infantry, artillery and so on. So General Gvero, by virtue of being a general, had the skills and knowledge to conduct military operations, that is, to lead troops in combat. Whether he had the experience, I don't know. I hope Gvero won't be offended, but I don't think he had, because from what I could see in his biography, he -- his only command responsibility was as platoon commander, and then he moved into a different area, professorial duties, lecturing duties, political responsibilities. I know that while I went to the military school of the JNA, part time he led a workshop on Marxism. I know that Gvero used to be a platoon commander, but whether he had ever been company commander or a brigade commander after that, I don't know. Gvero does, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you want to pursue the second part of your question, in which case you need to be specific, Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. In view of this answer, I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought so. So your next question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milovanovic, regarding the role and importance of General Gvero at the Main Staff, could his role be described as Mladic's eyes and ears, or Mladic's right hand, Mladic's associate who was also his confidant and most trusted man?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, let's take them one by one because you have put three or four questions in one. Let's start with the first one. With your permission, Mr. Krgovic, I'll do this myself. General, it's being put to you regarding the role and importance of General Gvero in the Main Staff. First question: Could his role be described as being Mladic's eyes and ears? If you can understand that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Mladic's eyes and ears, his eyes were the security administration and his ears were the intelligence administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. The second question, again regarding -- considering the role and importance of General Gvero, would you agree to the proposition that General Gvero was Mladic's right hand? Would you accept that proposition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I wouldn't. I would underestimate myself if I did. Mladic's right hand in conducting any operation was myself, nobody else. Anybody else would be left hands rather than the right hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the last question always in the same context of the role and importance of General Gvero in the Main Staff: Would you agree to the proposition that General Gvero could be considered as Mladic's associate who was also his confidant and most trusted man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll start with the last things first. General Gvero did not enjoy any special trust by General Mladic. I believe that General Mladic avoided having anybody among us in whom he would have placed most trust. He confided in me most because of the war. If General Gvero was his stooge, so to speak, and somebody who did everything for him, no, I wouldn't say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Back to you, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, are you familiar with the relationship between General Gvero and political bodies and especially Mr. Karadzic from the beginning of war to its end?
