According to my information, General Gvero and Karadzic, from the very outset were in permanent conflict and their relationship was rather bad throughout the war. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The special attitude of General Gvero towards the Supreme Commander was not noticeable. The attitude of the Supreme Command towards the Main Staff was rather volatile. At the beginning of the war, we were well-accepted by the Presidency. However, as the army was organised and as we started combat operations, attempts were made to ignore the role of the Main Staff, especially when the Supreme Command was established, of which I spoke yesterday. Nobody from the Main Staff made it to the Supreme Command. That's when we all realised that we represented some sort of opposition to the political leadership. We wanted the Supreme Command to provide funds for the army and for waging the war. However, the Supreme Command, throughout the war -- an analysis was made after the end of the war -- provided only 8 per cent of the total requirements of the army. As for the rest of the requirements, we made do as best as we could. We were fortunate to have the military industry under the authority of the army, which was adopted from the former JNA practice. So we could use the military industry products and trade them off with Yugoslavia. When it comes to the successes of the Republika Srpska army on the battlefields, we got increasingly attacked by the political leaders of Republika Srpska, by the individuals in that leadership. They would refer to us as the red gang because we had taken over the things that I spoke about yesterday. We had taken over the rules and the war rules from the former JNA, because, before the war, we had all served in the JNA, carrying the five-pointed stars on our hats. They called us Milosevic's mercenaries because the army of Yugoslavia was duty-bound to pay the officers' salaries. All these attacks against us came from the second echelon of the political leadership rather than directly from the three or four most important figures in the political leadership, and I'm talking about Karadzic, Koljevic, Plavsic and Krajisnik. These attacks came from their assistants and associates. This was a problem that General Gvero was supposed to resolve as the assistant commander for moral guidance, because this problem had a direct impact on the level of morale among the troops, and all this was done in order to avoid a direct clash between General Mladic and President Karadzic. The conflicts escalated in 1995 because of some political reasons. The political leadership of Republika Srpska accepted or decided to cede part of the territory that was under the Serb control, or, rather, they agreed to the return of the army from the parts of the territory under our control. For example, they agreed to the withdrawal of the army from Mount Igman and Mount Bjelasnica in August and September, 1993. Obviously, we objected to such decisions or such possibilities. We tried to overturn such decisions because we were the ones, we were the generals, who, for months before that, had forced the troops to take those positions in line with the directives of the Supreme Command. People had been killed, and then all of a sudden we were asked to abandon those areas and to make the troops go back. In 1995, in the month of April, there was an open conflict between the Main Staff and the Supreme Command, which was noticeable at the 15 April assembly in Sanski Most. The army was openly attacked for its alleged inactivity. However, nobody ever told us what further activities we were supposed to take, whether we should take more territory, whether we should abandon some territories. The army was considered unnecessary. It was frozen. The commander was attacked, as well as General Gvero, General Tolimir, General Djukic. I was skipped at that moment. I suppose I did not refrain from calling a spade a spade or something else. I don't know whether General Gvero personally came into conflict with Karadzic, but I know that before that, General Gvero was always duty-bound on behalf of the Main Staff to attend the sessions of the assembly of Republika Srpska, as well as the sessions of the government of Republika Srpska, if nothing else, then at least as an invited guest. After the assembly in Sanski Most, there was a change in the positions of General Mladic, and from then on he started sending either me or General Tolimir to the assembly, and if we were invited to the government sessions, then I would be sent instead of anybody else. This put me in a rather unfavourable position because the remainder of the Main Staff could have speculated about that and could have suspected that I had teamed up with the political leadership and that I was a traitor in the Main Staff, which was far from the truth. When I was naming the people who were directly attacked at the assembly in Sanski Most, the proof of that is the fact that very soon after that, there was an order issued by the Supreme Commander that some people who were members of the Main Staff should be retired, namely General Djukic, Gvero, Tolimir and I believe Ljubisa Beara. However, that order was not --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt the general, but perhaps we can get a date for that so we don't have to go back and cover this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The date of the Sanski Most --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The date that the issuing the orders related to the officers that were to be removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. General, if you could indicate the date, you're saying, "When I was naming the people who were directly attacked in the assembly at Sanski Most, the proof of that is the fact that very soon after that," we would like to know exactly or relatively when was that. You're saying that "there was an order issued by the Supreme Commander that some people who were members of the Main Staff should be retired, namely" and you mentioned three persons -- four persons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember the date, but that was very soon after the assembly meeting in Sanski Most. I can't be sure whether it was a month or two months later, but in any case, it was soon after the assembly meeting. However, I have not completed my answer with regard to this retirement business. Nobody from the Supreme Command ever asked for this order to be carried out. When the war was over, again an order was issued and these people were indeed retired, and a curiosity of that order was the fact that General Djordje Djukic was also retired, although he had died eight months prior to that order. And let me conclude. I don't know whether General Gvero entered into an open conflict with Karadzic, but I know that after that, Karadzic did not want to contact or get in touch with the four men that he had intended to send into retirement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Which means, that arises from your extensive answer, that after Sanski Most, General Gvero never went to the sessions of the assembly or the government?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I only know that I was sent to the government session. I was the one who went.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you go on with your next question, General, en passant, in answering the last question, you stated, "After the assembly in Sanski Most, there was a change in the positions of General Mladic and from then on, he started sending either me or General Tolimir to the assembly, and if we were invited, to the government sessions." Did he ever give you a reason for changing his previous position of sending General Gvero?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not aware of any reasons, and usually you never ask a commander why he makes a certain decision. A subordinate never questions his commander's decision. According to the military rule, you're just supposed to say, "Yes, I understand," if you do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, when you were talking about the way directives were drafted, yesterday to my learned friend's question, you answered that the person who commissioned so to speak the directive provides guidelines as to how the directive should be drafted. Do you remember having spoken about that? In a specific case, when the Supreme Command is the body that orders for a directive to be issued, it provides the background, the political background, as the basis for the drafting of the directive. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that. However, the person ordering a directive to be drafted, I said that that person provides guidelines rather than the framework for that directive. Usually, the guidelines that will go into this document, which is of strategic importance, are accompanied by the Supreme Command's assessment of the military and political situation in Republika Srpska, i.e., in the state to which the directive will be applied, in its immediate environment and in the world, taking into account the things that are of some significance for the army and the political situation in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Let's move on to another subject. In 1994 and 1995, if I'm not mistaken, and if I am, feel free to correct me, you were in the Bihac theatre of war conducting military operations. In that period, while you were active there, how did this theatre of war come into being at all? And what was the conduct of the UNPROFOR, the commander of the UNPROFOR regarding your activities, your operations?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Again, compound. He's talking about in 1994 and 1995. That's a very long period of time. If you could be specific, no problems, but several parts of this question, there is a huge period of time involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, point taken, I suppose. First I think we need to establish which period of time he was in the Bihac theatre, Bihac area, during military operations. Can you move to the rest of your question one by one, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, when the Muslim forces from the protected areas, and you spoke about this before, made incursion out of the zone, although they were not supposed to be there at all, and they captured 250 square kilometres of the Serb-controlled area, could you describe the conflict that ensued?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's obvious that I have to speak both faster and more concisely if I am ever to leave this place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. But you won't hold it against us, because you are the highest-ranking officer who has a lot of general knowledge on these matters, and we have to take avail of that and take advantage of you to help us clarify certain facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey, let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Same objection. It's the position of the Prosecutor that the Muslims were coming out of this enclave throughout. So it's a long time period he's talking about and it's not in dispute, of course, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it here I disagree with you because I think what Mr. Krgovic, and he'll correct me if I'm wrong, is referring -- specifically referring to is the event that the witness testified upon yesterday, where there was a surprise attack by the Muslims in the Bihac area, which then prompted the units under his control to counter-attack and also take possession of a particular -- but this is, if I am understanding you well, what you are referring the witness to, Mr. Krgovic, or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, but the reason I'm mentioning Bihac is one document that I would like to show the witness now. It's an intercept, in fact, between General Gvero -- could we show the witness P2374?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, I'm going to show you one intercept that was recorded by operators of the BH army, and in this conversation we hear General Gvero speaking to General Nicolai and he mentions deceit by the Muslim side regarding Bihac and Gorazde and the conduct of the UNPROFOR in such situations. That is the reason why I want you to comment on this passage.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is not in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P2374. If I may put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that will be quicker and the general -- okay. We found it. Yes, put it on the ELMO, usher. I think it's easier. All right. If it's under seal, it will remain under seal. We'll put it on the ELMO and we'll block broadcast of the document. So technicians, please, you're not to broadcast any image of this document while we proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the bottom part?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This underlined or rather highlighted part where General Gvero speaks of events in Bihac and Gorazde, can you tell us what happened to you that has to do with the conduct of the UNPROFOR when you were active in Bihac?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I cannot see the screen and I have no indication of when I can speak. And second, I understood your question and I don't need this document to answer it. Mr. President, may I speak now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood counsel as asking me to explain the conduct of the UNPROFOR in cases where the Muslim side made mistakes. I explained yesterday how the counterattack at Bihac occurred, and if I am allowed to speak about other people's mistakes, the mistake of the UNPROFOR was in allowing a protected area, where there shouldn't have been a single armed person, allowing a corps to be built up consisting of 22.000 men, the best-armed in the Balkans at that, which means that the UNPROFOR misinformed the Main Staff when it said it had disarmed Muslims around Bihac. I remember distinctly that they informed us of disarming three brigades in that area, namely the 505th Puzin Brigade, which was the most dangerous in that region. We believed the UNPROFOR and we suspended our front line facing the Una River. That's around Bihac. However, on the 23rd October, 1994, suddenly that 5th Muslim Corps, with those 22.000 men, crossed the Una River and burst into the territory under the control of Republika Srpska. Our 2nd Krajina Corps was taken by surprise, and even if it hadn't been taken by surprise, its strength was twice less. It was, in fact, around 14.000 in total, including logistics and everything. Over seven days, Muslims captured those 250 square kilometres, and that's the time when that intervention of our Supreme Command occurred. I spoke about that yesterday, and I believe I can skip it now. I hope I don't have to repeat it, not to waste time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. One moment to put all this in context, because the witness is referring to events that go back to October, 1994, and the intercept that you have referred the witness to is dated, at least if that's correct, 11th July 1995, and refers to events that are completely different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have to note that for the record, it is in English page 2 of P2347A. It should be page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Kwon. The question that you put to the witness referred specifically to this intercept. This intercept is dated 11th July and it obviously, at least from the face -- on the face of it, refers to events that had just happened. There is nothing from this document that indicates or even leads us to imagine for a moment that it refers to the events that occurred in October of the previous year that the witness has just referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know which passage you are looking at, but we have here words ascribed to General Gvero. He's describing events that took place before in Bihac and Gorazde and he says, "Let General Nicolai be reminded that the same thing had already happened in Bihac and Gorazde."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It should be two pages, 2347A.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, I'll try to put a leading question to cut this short. Is it correct that the moment you approached Bihac, when you took up your initial position, in view of the reports that you had --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear anything because of the shuffling in the microphones. Could counsel please repeat?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat the question for the sake of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, is it correct that when you returned and recovered previous positions and approached Bihac, at that moment, even though you had not shelled Bihac and you had made no counterattack, you were bombed by NATO aviation, there were NATO air strikes against you, although you were not given a map of the protected area with no indication of how far you can go?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My trouble, when I completed the task given me by the Supreme Command is not interesting to this Court, but the fact is I didn't know what to do, to go on or to stop. At that time the army of Republika Srpska under my command had come dangerously close to Bihac. Bihac was a protected area, although that's where the attack against us came from. I asked on parallel channels, both from the Supreme Command and from General Mladic, a reply: What was I to do? I asked the Supreme Command because I was executing directly the orders of the Supreme Commander, and I sought General Mladic's explanation due to the normal military subordination because I was supposed to address my immediate superior. General Mladic's reply was to stop, pending further instructions from the Supreme Command. And I stopped. In the meantime, I received a call from General Rose, then the force commander for Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he told me that I must not attack Bihac. I answered that it was not my problem and it was not my decision, it was up to the Supreme Command. He also said that if I continued my attack, my advance on Bihac, there would be air strikes against me. However, something weird was going on, some sort of negotiations were going on between the Republic of Serbian Krajina, to give you a better idea that was this state-like creation led by Milan Martic, so those negotiations were between Milan Martic and the state of Croatia in Zagreb. So I understood Rose's threat in two different ways. I understood that if I go on, they will attack me but I didn't expect to be attacked even if I stayed where I was. However, he attacked me on the 21st, the 22nd and the 23rd November. I am quoting those dates because the 21st was my birthday and I joked with my friends that it was a very nice birthday card from Rose. He bombed me for three days. I was unable to establish contact with him, although I had informed the command and General Mladic, and I don't know what was going on at their end. At any rate, the air strikes stopped on the 23rd. On the 24th, the evening of the 24th, that is one day after the cessation of air strikes, I received an envelope from General Rose and I thought it was some sort of letter because he had promised me a letter of intent, although he had promised it would be a menacing one, but when I opened the envelope it was a topographic map with the boundaries of the protected area of Bihac drawn in. Until then such boundaries did not exist, like the boundaries of Tuzla or the boundaries of Sarajevo protected areas did not exist. I believe that Tuzla and Sarajevo do not have such boundaries to this day. The boundaries of the Bihac secure zone was drawn to coincide exactly with the front positions of my forces, where they were in Bihac at the time. So I did not violate the protected area. But what was curious was that this was signed at the Security Council at -- and now there is a time difference between the US and Europe, but it was signed in the morning of the 24th November, and I received it that evening. But it doesn't matter whether it was signed in the morning or the evening. What matters is that it was signed after the cessation of attacks and I believe that counsel was trying to get precisely at that. I think that my troops were attacked illegally, unlawfully. And a similar thing had already happened a couple of months before that in Gorazde. Gorazde was also a protected area. From that area, one commander, I believe Sejdic was his name. General Pandurevic knows him very well because he's the one who fought him, this Sedic took out of the Gorazde protected area a unit of 750 men, passing through UNPROFOR lines, passing through our lines, and in the area of Mount Sjemec, they attacked very violently, very brutally, Serb villages, killing I don't know how many people. Pandurevic's unit found them and engaged them but they were only able to stop them, and just at that moment, General Mladic arrived in the theatre of war, coming back from his daughter's funeral. He went directly to Sjemec and launched a spontaneous action to expel that group, just as I did later on in Bihac. The Muslims informed the entire world through the media that Serbs had destroyed such and such a number of houses in Gorazde, killing so many people, and the UNPROFOR threatened air strikes against Serb troops around Gorazde from NATO aircraft. General Rose was the force commander of the UNPROFOR. Again, he didn't believe Muslim propaganda. Instead he went to Gorazde himself. I didn't know what he found there, but in the book he wrote later, the title of the book being, "The Bosnia Mission," he wrote that he had in fact seen destroyed houses but houses that had been destroyed two years before in 1992, in the first conflicts between Serbs and Muslims. And on the 21st of April, air strikes began.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's enough. Please, General, I didn't stop you, of course, because in a way, all this was important for the Defence, who didn't try to stop you, either, but I would suggest that you try to keep your answers as brief an as possible because we too would like you to leave The Hague and go back to your country this weekend. Otherwise, I see no chance of reaching the end of your testimony this week. Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, as far as I'm aware, concerning these incursions launched by Muslims out of protected area, and the killings of UNPROFOR members, the Muslims were never punished for that, were they?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 5th Muslim Corps from Bihac was never punished. I don't know about the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By whom would they have been punished, Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By NATO air strikes, the same that applied to the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But this is what -- that is what Mr. Krgovic meant, and your answer remains the same, General, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, let me ask you briefly, you have already explained part of it in the examination-in-chief when you were explaining the way documents were signed. When a document that has been produced is submitted for transmission by teletype, a certain person is indicated in the signature spot indicating their rank and title. If that person does not sign in their own hand to verify the document, the person receiving the document, if somebody has signed with the prefix "for," this handwritten inscription "for" is not seen on the receiving end. You only see the typed name of the person in the signature line; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct, and I believe that when I was answering the Prosecutor, the same answer applies to the Defence. I don't see the need to duplicate questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And what if you put the indication "SR" at the bottom of the document? Does that mean that a person indicated on the signature line signed the document personally in their own hand?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He answered that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General Milovanovic, let me ask you this. You know General Gvero. I will now show you a document from 1992. Can we show the witness document 6D129? This is a document from 1992 where General Gvero, in his capacity of assistant for morale, discusses certain matters, how certain actions affect the morale of troops, and how members of other ethnic communities and members of the UNPROFOR and other organisations should be treated. Could you please look at this document carefully? General Gvero says here that even before this, he had already drawn attention several times to the need to stop retributions, prevent retributions against innocent population, destruction, looting, arson, et cetera, because such actions blemish the image of the Serb soldier and that innocent people should not be treated like that simply because they are not Serbs. Can you see this passage? Is it consistent with your impression? Do you believe that General Gvero really believed what he was saying here, that that was his personal position?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the document. Very likely General Gvero stands behind this document, if he signed it, because I don't see the signature line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can we scroll down so we can see the signature?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the signature of General Gvero. I don't see the famous letters SR, which means in his own hand. What do you want me to do? To confirm this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No. My question was a bit broader. What is written in this document, in your personal belief, does it -- it really express General Gvero's own ideas, the way he also shared them with you at meetings?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Let me draw your attention to one passage that begins with the words, "Treatment of domestic and foreign journalists, members of the UNPROFOR, the International Red Cross must be cordial, humane and perfectly decent in all situations. They should be accommodated and enabled to work unhindered and every attempt should be made to gain their sympathy, to win them over."

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that. I would never personally use the word "cordial" or "cordially." I would say that the treatment should be decent, fair, and in keeping with international standards and laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But you see that. Does this also express your personal position?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the position of the Main Staff, not my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question, General. As long as we're talking about documents, every sector had their own reference number and the number of your sector was 03, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I think I will finish before the break. Just one more question. Are you aware that one part of General Gvero's sector -- I mean information and legal affairs -- were based in a hotel in Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The press centre was based at the hotel -- or rather, not at the hotel. In Han Pijesak in some other building, I believe it was the municipal building. Where it was relocated in end 1994 or end 1995, I don't know, and I don't know whether anybody from Gvero's sector was relocated from Crna Rijeka to Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And although were you not there in the summer of 1995, are you aware that in that office that you marked as Gvero's, Tolimir occupied and used that office while he was there with his wife? The office that you designated as Gvero's.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Tolimir was in one of those rooms with his wife, sometime during the war. I explained yesterday to the Prosecutor that Gvero was relocated from what we called the blue room to the adjacent room. I don't know whether Tolimir was accordingly moved one room further. I don't know. I didn't spend my time during the war monitoring such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But Gvero's service was moved to Han Pijesak and Gvero himself got one room in the barracks, from March to October 1995, you were not there, but maybe you know.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Who is going next? Although I think we will have the break now. But it will be you, Madam Fauveau. You requested three and a half hours. How much of that do you still require?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to stick to the three and a half hours, but I'll make an effort to finish as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just before we break, then, Beara, Mr. Ostojic, how much time -- you asked for an hour and three-quarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thus far we think we are going to reduce it, so we would like to reserve 45 minutes to an hour, but we may not have any questions depending on the next day or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ostojic. Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think we are still in the region of an hour or a little more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. We have no questions at this time, but I would like to reserve ten minutes for one question which I think will be asked by somebody else. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the meantime, for the record, I have to note that on page 55, line 18, I meant 2374A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Kwon. We'll have a break of 25 minutes and we will then reconvene for the last session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau? Perhaps you can introduce yourself to the witness and proceed. And then we continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: My name is Natacha Fauveau-Ivanovic. I appear here for General Miletic. Could we show the witness P2828? It's a diagram that the Prosecutor showed him sometime ago. Can we show the part lower, a bit higher now, please? Just a little bit higher? That's it. Thank you. Sir, you said that General Miletic was in the room marked 5 when you were not there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: We can also see the name Miletic appearing in room number 3. Is it true that General Miletic was very often present in room number 3 at times when you were there as well as at times when you weren't there?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because the operations centre was part of the operations administration headed by General Miletic, and this is where the working conditions were the best. He had a broad scope for work there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Earlier today you've told us that a large number of people were accommodated in that room, including the assistant commanders.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not assistant commanders but their -- but his deputies or other persons appointed by the assistant commanders. Those were duty officers, the duty team, that had to have representatives of all sectors and administrations. And the assistant commanders were there when the staff meetings took place at the operations centre because that room was the largest, the biggest room, in that house.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In any case, there were moments when assistant commanders were in that room temporarily?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You've told us that your extension was 155. Is it true that extension 155 was connected both with room number 5, as well as room number 3, and also with some other rooms that belonged to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for this intervention. This should have been said earlier today when I was answering the Prosecutor's questions. As I was preparing for this testimony, the Prosecutor and I discussed this extension, number 155, and he asked me another question. The first question was whether this was my extension, to which I said yes, which I repeated earlier today, and his second question was as follows: Could this extension be used by anybody else? And I explained it to him. I was expecting that second question today. It never was asked. So I would like to tell you now, that this extension was connected with the room under the dotted line, which was my rest room, and it was also parallelly connected with room number 3, which is the operations centre where there were always more than ten people present, like I've explained earlier today, and it was parallelly connected with the operations hall in the underground command post so if anybody wanted to talk to me and if I was not in my office, if I was not in my bedroom, i.e., the operator the switchboard to try to connect me in the bedroom. If I wasn't there, then he would connect the call to the operations centre. There was always somebody there. Whoever was closest to the telephone would answer the call.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it correct that in urgent cases and particularly when there was a meeting going on, if an assistant commander who was attending the meeting in room number 3 and had to talk to an assistant who was underground, that person would leave the message to the assistant and ask them to call extension 155?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they left messages or not but they could get connected through extension 155 if they were at the operations centre at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Thus, if a message was call 155, the only thing we can conclude that the call was not necessarily for General Miletic but for anybody who was supposed to answer; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That telephone became a public phone in the General Staff, in the Main Staff, very soon after it was connected.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday you spoke about directive number 7. Can the witness please be shown Exhibit number P5? Can the witness please be shown page 21, in English page 15? Can we display the lower part, the signature part? Thank you. Yesterday you told us that this directive had been signed by the Supreme Commander, Radovan Karadzic, and that it had been drafted by Radivoje Miletic. Is it correct that Colonel Miletic was supposed to write in the directive whatever had been decided by Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And he could not omit any Karadzic's decisions from the directive?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not allowed to do that. He was not allowed to omit anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we say that General Miletic did not have any room for adding something to the contents of the directive? He could not make any decision with regard to the contents of the directive?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not allowed to change the contents of the directive that were provided to him by Karadzic. The only thing he could do was to word, to phrase, the wording of the directive in -- so as to meet all the linguistic requirements, the requirements that we spoke about earlier this morning, the conjunction words, the grammar -- fine grammar points.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yesterday you went into great lengths about directive writing and you said that there was a team of people that were in charge of drafting directives in general terms. Is it true that this team consisted of several people and that whoever was the author of the directive, and in this case, this was Colonel Miletic, was provided all the elements by these people that would enable him to phrase the directive?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The drafting of all written documents to be issued by the Main Staff, relative to any combat activities, is in the -- within the purview of the operate -- operations administration. There is no dedicated team that is appointed to do that, unless there is a specific need to appoint a dedicated team. All the other sectors and administrations of the Main Staff were duty-bound in this specific case, in the case of directive number 7, to provide Miletic with their respective positions and opinions. Since this directive was drafted for the Supreme Command, and at the request of the Supreme Command, Miletic could, but did not have to, consult with the assistants of the commander. The situation was different when a document to be issued by the Main Staff was being drafted. Then it was his duty to consult the commander's assistants.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And since we are talking about a directive to be issued by the Supreme Command, you were saying that he was not duty-bound to consult with the assistants to the commander. Is it true that he did not have to consult them because all the guidelines for this directive had been provided to him by the Supreme Command, i.e., the Supreme Commander?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This should have been the case. I don't know whether Miletic consulted anybody. If I had been in his shoes, I would have done it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we now show the witness page 15 of this directive, which is number 10 in English? Can we display the lower part of the document? Yes -- or no. Can we see the part that is in bold letters? Sir, the part that starts with the words, "the Drina Corps," describes the duties of the Drina Corps the way the Supreme Commander, Radovan Karadzic, saw them. Are these the duties that the Supreme Command entrusted the Drina Corps with?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, that will be the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Based on what you've just told us, even if General Miletic did not agree with these tasks and duties, he still had to incorporate them in the directive; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And if the general had omitted this part from the draft directive, Radovan Karadzic could have added that after having read the directive and before signing it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You yourself have told us that you were not present in the Main Staff when this directive was drafted. Is it true that you don't know whether General Miletic objected to the decision made by Radovan Karadzic on carrying out this task? Did he oppose Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but even if he had, it would have been in vain.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we now show the witness Exhibit number 5D361? The document that you are going to see in a minute is another directive, directive 7-1 which was issued by the Main Staff of the army. Can we please show the fifth page, both in the B/C/S version as well as in the English version? Sir, can you see the passage 5.3, starting with the words, "The Drina Corps" where the tasks of the Drina Corps are defined according to the ideas of the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska army? Is it correct that this directive issued by the Main Staff of the VRS does not adopt the tasks of the Drina Corps in the way they were defined by the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Here, the commander of the Main Staff took the responsibility upon himself and changed the decision of the Supreme Commander. Here, I don't see General Mladic ordering incursion of the Serbian army into the enclaves. He, rather, wants to isolate the 2nd Corps, probably due to the fact that in Sarajevo the Muslim offensive was raging with a view to de-blocking Sarajevo. In other words, he wanted to tie up the forces of the 2nd Muslim Corps in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true that based on the information that you had, and you were the chief of the Main Staff of VRS, not for a single moment in the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina was the civilian population targeted by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civilian population was never targeted by the VRS, save for in some individual cases when we came under the artillery fire by the Muslim army from an inhabited area. We believed that the Muslims also adhered by the Geneva Conventions and that they knew that they should not mix the military target with the civilian targets.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to ask you something about the humanitarian convoys and UNPROFOR convoys. Is it true that based on the information that you had, the position of the VRS towards the humanitarian convoys did not change after the directive number 7 had been issued?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if anything changed. In the part of the theatre of war where I was, there were no enclaves and no humanitarian aid arrived at the civilian authorities. I don't know what was going on in eastern Bosnia with regard to the humanitarian aid. Where I was, there were no humanitarian aid convoys.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, you were in the Main Staff, in the command, up to the end of May, 1995, or in any case, you were there in March, April and May, 1995. During that period of time, did you notice any restrictions on the number of humanitarian convoys?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On whose part?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: On the part of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime in 1994, a committee was established in Republika Srpska for humanitarian aid, and thereby the responsibility for supplying humanitarian aid was shifted from the Main Staff to civilian authorities. Heading that committee was the vice-president of the republic, Nikola Koljevic, and I believe that the committee also comprised one or two officers. These officers conveyed the decisions of the committee to the Main Staff so that we can suspend any combat activities on routes through which humanitarian aid was supplied or was to be supplied.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to show you several documents concerning humanitarian aid, but before that, is it correct that all the convoys were humanitarian convoys and UNPROFOR convoys were controlled from the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the agreement between the UNPROFOR force that secured humanitarian convoys and the army of Republika Srpska, all convoys were inspected at check-points or at points of entry into protected areas. The inspection was performed by mixed groups made up of members of the VRS and members of the UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true that during those inspections and even by other means, you sometimes found out that convoys were abused in the sense that they transported forbidden goods?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The non-governmental organisation supplying humanitarian aid, namely the UNHCR, was duty-bound to provide UNPROFOR with a list of materials or materiel entering the enclave, and the UNPROFOR was duty-bound to transmit the list to us, and at the beginning, while we still trusted each other -- or rather, while we trusted the UNPROFOR still, inspections were only partial. For instance, we would say, "Let's inspect one in five or one in seven trucks," and then if something is discovered in this random check, the convoy would be stopped and inspected in its entirety. Anything that was not on the list accompanying the convoy would be excluded, removed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to show you an exhibit which is in English but I'll read it to you. There is only one sentence that interests me. It's 5D390. For your information, it's a document of the United Nations. It's in fact a transcript of a meeting that representatives of the VRS had with the UNPROFOR on 9 April 1993. Could we move to page 2? Paragraph 1, the second sentence in that paragraph and that is as follows: "[In English] The issue of discovery on the previous day at Sarajevo of approximately 30.000 rounds of ammunition, hidden on an UNHCR convoy escorted by UNPROFOR, was raised early." [Interpretation] Is it true that it was strictly prohibited to transport munitions and weapons in humanitarian convoys?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to Article 60, I believe it was 60, of the first protocol of the Geneva Conventions of the UN, there are four clauses regulating the status or, rather, the way protected areas operate. One of those clauses prohibits the existence of -- or the presence of any kind of military equipment, weapons, munitions, uniforms, anything that symbolises any accoutrements of the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And in the case like here that UNHCR transported ammunition, and that was not an isolated case, there were others --

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No particular evidence is needed. I spoke yesterday and earlier today about the 5th Muslim Corps that was disarmed and grew in Bihac to a size of 22.000 soldiers. We were informed by the UNPROFOR in 1993 that Srebrenica was disarmed, that military installations had been converted into civilian facilities, that any soldiers that had been left behind in Srebrenica were disarmed, and still the 28th Infantry Division of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina came into being in Srebrenica. The same thing happened in Zepa. We were informed that 900 infantry weapons had been removed and that the armed force was disarmed, and still a brigade called the 4th of June was formed there with a strength of 1200. In the Gorazde enclave, the protected area had a diameter of three kilometres, the agreed protected area. However, the 81st Infantry Division of the Muslim army was born there with about 6.000 to 6.500 men. So there is no need for any evidence to prove the violations occurring in the supply of humanitarian aid. Weapons and ammunition could not find any other way into enclaves except through the combat disposition of the UNPROFOR, on humanitarian convoys. True, there was an operation sometime in 1994, namely to supply humanitarian aid by air lift. It was known under the code name parachute. The humanitarian aid was dropped by parachute into enclaves from rather high altitudes by night, but either the pilots did not adjust the altitude properly or it was disrupted by the wind. In any case, sometimes the parachute would find its way into territory controlled by the VRS, and I remember the outcry that resulted when munitions for a machine-gun, 12.7 millimetres, was found in flour sacks dropped by such a parachute. Whenever we detected something like that, we would inform the UNPROFOR, ask them to pay attention, but whenever we discovered something like that, the Main Staff sent notifications in writing to subordinated units, mainly the units of the Drina Corps and the Herzegovina Corps because it was these two that controlled access to enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You've already explained to me the procedure of passage of convoys and notifications. I just want you to look at the document to confirm that stipulates these procedures. It's 5D378. Is it true that it's a document of the Main Staff of the VRS of 3rd April 1993?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And in paragraph 2, we read something about notification of convoys, and then in the third paragraph, it says that convoys have to be notified four hours prior to departure -- sorry, 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot find it this very minute. I don't know what you call first or second paragraph, but I don't need to, after all. It's true, the UNPROFOR was duty-bound to announce departure of convoys 24 hours in advance. But let me emphasise, on the 3rd of April the enclaves or rather protected areas within enclaves had not been established yet at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'm perfectly in agreement, but still there were controls, inspections and the procedure of notification was in place?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that procedure continued to apply after the protected areas were established.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true that -- we discussed ammunitions and weapons -- that there were frequently problems with fuel and there was a black market and the UNHCR and UNPROFOR transported fuel in enclaves or in any case under Muslim -- in territories under Muslim control?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot claim that it is true about the UNPROFOR, but it is true of UNHCR. I personally believe that at the beginning, it was contraband and criminal activity of individuals. Somebody would go into the enclave with a full tank, then empty the tank of a certain amount of fuel. In any case, it was on an individual basis at the beginning. When we found out, and that sort of thing is very difficult to find out, we notified the UNPROFOR and I'm afraid that was a mistake. It was a mistake to inform them of this petty crime, because we gave them an idea on how to spread it, put it on a wider scale. So that in addition to those escorting UNHCR convoys, UNPROFOR soldiers began the same practice and the whole thing culminated when it was discovered that certain vehicles, in the course of preparing convoys, have a double bottom or rather their tanks, fuel tanks, had double bottoms. That already amounted to organised crime, both on the part of the UNPROFOR and on the part of the UNHCR. But by that time we no longer trusted the UNPROFOR or the UNHCR, and we introduced very strict controls, checks and inspections. That meant inspecting every vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Just before we adjourn, can we show document 5D374 to the witness? It's an order from the Main Staff of the VRS of 30th September 1993. And there, in paragraphs 1 and 2, this order discusses the problem in fuel transported by humanitarian convoys. That's paragraph 1. And paragraph 2 deals with more strict controls of fuel imports through humanitarian convoys.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And perhaps just before we adjourn, we can show another document to the witness, 5D372.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In fact, Mr. President, I was perhaps too optimistic, because on the other hand, tomorrow I think I need only the first session. I'll finish before the first break tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That means we stand a chance of finishing with the witness tomorrow. It also means that you need to have the next one prepared. So, General, we are going to adjourn. We'll meet again tomorrow morning at 9.00 like today. Same advisory as yesterday: You're not to discuss the subject matter of your testimony with anyone between now and tomorrow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
